headline: Late July at Washington: this is why we don't wait for the other canyons
subhead: Yellowfin have been on the troll wall since the Fourth, and the calendar says we've still got a month of this before the wahoo show up to complicate things.
body_markdown:
By the third week of July I've stopped being surprised by anything Washington does — I've fished this piece of bottom long enough to know it runs its own calendar, usually two to three weeks ahead of Hudson and Wilmington, and this season is no exception. We were seeing quality yellowfin activity here before most boats had even splashed for their first canyon run, and now that we're deep into the settled summer pattern, the fish have simply stayed put. That's not luck. That's the shelf break doing what it does at Washington every year once the Gulf Stream noses in close and the warm water sets up shop along the edge instead of sliding past it.

Right now the money water is stacking along the northeast wall, out toward the 200-fathom curve, with the temp break holding steady in that upper 70s to near-80-degree range. That's the number that matters more than any single buoy reading — when you find that break sitting tight against structure instead of smeared out over open water, you've found where the bait's going to hold, and where the bait holds, the yellowfin hold. I've been marking the strongest concentrations where the color goes from that dirty green Gulf Stream edge to clean cobalt blue, usually somewhere in the 100 to 150 fathom transition before you even hit the true canyon depths. Troll that seam with a spread of cedar plugs and small Ilanders — green/yellow and pink/white have both been drawing strikes — and you're going to find fish in the 40 to 60 pound class without needing to run all the way to the eastern wall.

The chunk bite has been the more consistent producer for the boats willing to commit to an overnight. Set up on the edge where the current is pushing bait against structure, deploy a slow butterflied bunker chunk on a long leader — 6 to 8 feet of 50 or 60-pound fluoro, small hook, no swivel showing — and let it drift down naturally in the chum slick. That's been putting bigger fish in the box, yellowfin pushing 70 pounds, along with the occasional bigeye showing up in the middle of the night bite when the moon's dark enough to keep the deep-water feeders comfortable coming up. We're past full moon now and heading toward the new phase, which historically has been good to us here — less moonlight up top usually means a better late-night chunk bite as the bigeye push shallower to feed.

Mahi have been the bonus fish all month, and they haven't slowed down. Any bit of floating structure — a lobster pot buoy, a mat of sargassum, even a stray piece of dock debris — is worth a look and a few pitched baits. Small feathers or a strip of squid on a light spinning rod will get you a quick mixed bag while the bigger baits keep soaking for tuna. I wouldn't plan a whole trip around them, but they've saved more than a few slow mornings out here.

White marlin have been scattered through the same water as the yellowfin, mostly showing on the troll spread rather than committing hard, which is typical for this stage of the season. A couple of teams have had multiple bites in a day without converting all of them — that's just white marlin being white marlin in late July. Drop back a natural bait quickly if you see one crash the pattern and give it time before you set the hook.

Wahoo have been quiet so far, which tracks with where we are in the season. Washington usually doesn't turn on wahoo-heavy until we get into that August water — once the break sharpens up further and the current really starts ripping across the edge. I wouldn't be running dedicated wahoo bombs yet, but keep a couple of high-speed lures in the middle of the spread just in case; they show up early some years and this canyon has surprised me before.

We flagged this pattern building last week — said the yellowfin bite would hold given the settled high pressure, and that's exactly what's happened. No storms to break up the structure, no cold water intrusions to scatter the bait, just steady clean water sitting on the edge and fish stacking up on it day after day. That kind of stability is rare enough in late July that you don't question it, you just fish it.

Looking ahead, I don't see a reason for this to fall apart in the next week unless the weather pattern shifts. The high pressure's been parked over the mid-Atlantic long enough that the thermal structure out here is mature and settled rather than fresh and jumpy, which usually means the fish stay committed to the same stretches of the wall instead of wandering. If I had a boat and a weather window this week, I'd run straight to that northeast wall temp break first, work it with the troll spread for two or three hours to locate the pod, then switch over to the chunk and sit on it through the evening bite into the night. That's been the winning one-two punch all month, and there's no read on the water right now telling me to change it. Keep an eye on the moon phase heading into early August — as it darkens up further, I'd expect the overnight bigeye bite to get another notch stronger before wahoo season properly kicks off behind it.
